reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Suspect this diagnosis when a patient with atopic dermatitis (or another barrier-disrupting skin disease) suddenly deteriorates with a widespread painful eruption
The hallmark lesions are numerous monomorphic punched-out erosions and clustered vesicles that may coalesce and crust, often concentrated over previously eczematous skin of the face, neck, and trunk
Fever, malaise, and tender lymphadenopathy commonly accompany the skin findings and signal systemic involvement
Herpes simplex virus (usually type 1) is the most frequent cause, but coxsackie and vaccinia viruses can produce a similar picture
Treat empirically with systemic antiviral therapy without waiting for confirmation, since delay increases the risk of dissemination and complications
Take viral swabs from the base of a de-roofed vesicle for PCR or culture, and consider bacterial swabs because secondary staphylococcal or streptococcal infection is common
Ocular involvement warrants urgent ophthalmology review to prevent herpetic keratitis and visual loss
Avoid or minimise topical corticosteroids and calcineurin inhibitors during the acute infective phase, and be cautious about attributing all worsening simply to an eczema flare
reference.pathophysiology: Eczema herpeticum arises when a cutaneous viral infection, most often herpes simplex virus, spreads rapidly across skin whose barrier and immune defences are already compromised. In atopic dermatitis the combination of filaggrin-related barrier dysfunction, reduced antimicrobial peptide expression, and a T-helper-2 skewed immune milieu allows the virus to breach the epidermis and disseminate widely rather than remain localised. Viral cytopathic effect produces ballooning keratinocyte degeneration and the characteristic uniform vesicles and erosions. Viraemia and secondary bacterial superinfection can drive systemic upset, and in severe cases multi-organ involvement.
additionalDifferentials: Impetiginised or bacterially superinfected eczema flare
Primary varicella or disseminated herpes zoster
additionalInvestigations: Viral PCR or culture from vesicle fluid or a de-roofed lesion base
Direct immunofluorescence or Tzanck smear where rapid bedside clues are needed
Bacterial swabs and cultures for co-existent staphylococcal or streptococcal infection
Blood tests to assess systemic upset, including markers of infection and hydration status
Ophthalmological slit-lamp examination when periocular lesions are present
redFlags: Dermatological emergency: initiate urgent systemic antiviral therapy rather than delaying for laboratory confirmation
Periocular or ocular lesions raising the risk of sight-threatening herpetic keratitis
Signs of systemic sepsis, dehydration, or haemodynamic instability, particularly in infants
Rapidly extending eruption or involvement of extensive body surface area
Immunocompromised host in whom dissemination and visceral involvement are more likely
reference.prognosis: With prompt antiviral treatment most patients recover well, but untreated or delayed cases can be complicated by widespread dissemination, secondary bacterial sepsis, ocular damage, and, rarely, death; recurrences can occur with subsequent eczema flares.
pitfalls: Mistaking the eruption for an ordinary eczema exacerbation and simply intensifying topical steroids
Delaying antiviral therapy while awaiting swab results
Overlooking eye involvement and its risk to vision
Failing to consider and treat concurrent bacterial infection
Underestimating severity in infants and immunosuppressed patients
management: Start systemic antiviral therapy with aciclovir or valaciclovir empirically and promptly without awaiting confirmation, using intravenous aciclovir for severe, extensive or systemically unwell cases
Take viral PCR swabs from the base of a de-roofed vesicle to confirm herpes simplex, but do not delay treatment
Treat secondary bacterial superinfection with antibacterials covering staphylococci and streptococci, guided by bacterial swabs
Provide supportive care with analgesia, fluids and attention to hydration and systemic upset, admitting if severe
Obtain urgent ophthalmology slit-lamp review for periocular lesions to detect and treat herpetic eye disease
Cautiously manage the underlying atopic dermatitis by restoring the barrier with emollients and minimising topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors during the acute infection
Advise on recognising recurrence with future eczema flares and seeking prompt re-treatment, and refer to dermatology
